rows.source: HSE personal protective equipment
rows.verified: Employers must protect workers from health and safety risks and provide required PPE free of charge when the risk assessment shows it is needed.

rows.source: HSE personal protective equipment
rows.verified: PPE can include safety helmets, gloves, eye or hearing protection, high-visibility clothing, safety footwear and harnesses.

rows.source: HSE personal protective equipment
rows.verified: Respiratory protective equipment is a form of PPE used to reduce inhalation of dust, mist, gas or fume.

rows.source: HSE personal protective equipment
rows.verified: PPE may be needed where hazards remain after engineering controls and safe systems of work have been applied.

rows.source: HSE personal protective equipment
rows.verified: PPE must be assessed before use to make sure it is fit for purpose.

rows.source: HSE personal protective equipment
rows.verified: PPE must be maintained and stored properly.

rows.source: HSE personal protective equipment
rows.verified: Workers must receive instructions on safe PPE use and must use the equipment correctly.

rows.source: HSE personal protective equipment
rows.verified: Employers must provide sufficient information, instruction and training, and supplied PPE should comply with product-supply legislation.

rows.source: HSE personal protective equipment
rows.verified: The suitable PPE depends on the actual hazard, fit, compatibility, wearer and remaining risk after higher-level controls.

rows.source: HSE personal protective equipment
rows.verified: PPE evidence is worker-, task- and equipment-specific and is not an exact parcel-level safety probability.

rows.source: HSE workplace temperature and thermal comfort
rows.verified: Employers should provide a reasonable working temperature in indoor workrooms, usually at least 16°C or 13°C where work involves rigorous physical effort.

rows.source: HSE workplace temperature and thermal comfort
rows.verified: Where a comfortable temperature cannot be maintained throughout a workroom, local heating or cooling can be provided.

rows.source: HSE workplace temperature and thermal comfort
rows.verified: Rest facilities may be needed for hot work or for warming workers in cold environments.

rows.source: HSE workplace temperature and thermal comfort
rows.verified: Heating systems should not emit dangerous or offensive levels of fumes into the workplace.

rows.source: HSE workplace temperature and thermal comfort
rows.verified: Warm-condition controls can include ventilation, air conditioning, shading, cold drinking water and moving workstations away from heat.

rows.source: HSE workplace temperature and thermal comfort
rows.verified: Cold-condition controls can include adequate heating, reduced draughts, protective clothing and limiting exposure time.

rows.source: HSE workplace temperature and thermal comfort
rows.verified: Thermal comfort depends on air temperature, radiant temperature, air movement, humidity, clothing insulation and work rate.

rows.source: HSE workplace temperature and thermal comfort
rows.verified: Air temperature alone is not a valid indicator of thermal comfort or heat stress.

rows.source: HSE workplace temperature and thermal comfort
rows.verified: There is no single legal maximum workplace temperature because workplaces, processes, clothing and work rates differ.

rows.source: HSE workplace temperature and thermal comfort
rows.verified: Temperature evidence is time-, task-, environment- and worker-specific and is not a permanent parcel-level safety probability.
